title: Oosterweel Link (Antwerp)
subtitle: Closing the Antwerp ring road, one rising estimate at a time
intended: Close the Antwerp ring road (R1) and improve mobility around the city, as the central works of the Flemish 'Toekomstverbond' programme.
actual: Cost estimates have risen over successive years. In March 2026 the effective construction cost was put at €10 billion (2024 price level); the project's projected accounting value is €13.6 billion by 2034, and the Court of Audit warns the financing is 'strongly problematic'.
summary: The Oosterweelverbinding is the final phase of closing Antwerp's ring road (R1), part of the Flemish 'Toekomstverbond' programme and delivered through the project company Lantis (formerly BAM) on behalf of the Flemish Government. In its March 2026 progress report to the Flemish Parliament, Lantis and the responsible minister put the effective construction cost at €10 billion at 2024 price level, described as unchanged from the previous year. Lantis's financial model projects an accounting value of €13.6 billion by 2034 at full completion, a figure that (per the government) reflects subordinated lending, risk financing and indexation rather than additional construction cost. The Court of Audit (Rekenhof) has repeatedly reported that the financing is 'strongly problematic', flagging a projected financing shortfall of about €2.3 billion above a loan ceiling already raised from €3.6 billion to €6.7 billion, and warning that expected toll revenues after 2034 are overestimated. Earlier estimates for the project were reported to be far lower (around €7 billion); an exact original budget figure is not documented here.

title: Agusta-Dassault affair
subtitle: Defence contracts, socialist party coffers, and the highest court in the land
institution: Belgian federal government · Court of Cassation (Cour de cassation / Hof van Cassatie)
intended: Award Belgian defence contracts in the late 1980s: helicopters from the Italian firm Agusta and electronic countermeasures for Belgian F-16s from the French firm Dassault.
actual: The contracts were accompanied by bribes paid to the Flemish and Francophone socialist parties. When the scheme surfaced in the 1990s, senior ministers and party officials were prosecuted. Because sitting and former ministers were involved, they were tried directly by the Court of Cassation. On 23 December 1998 the court convicted all twelve defendants of corruption and related offences.
summary: In the late 1980s the Belgian government awarded defence contracts to Agusta (helicopters) and Dassault (F-16 electronic countermeasures). In exchange, bribes were channelled to the Flemish socialist party (SP) and the Francophone socialist party (PS). Because the accused included sitting and former government ministers, who enjoyed a constitutional privilege of jurisdiction, they were tried directly by the Court of Cassation sitting as a trial court, in a single, non-appealable proceeding. On 23 December 1998 the court convicted all twelve defendants. Former Economy and Foreign Affairs minister Willy Claes, who had already resigned as NATO Secretary-General in 1995, was convicted of passive corruption and received a three-year suspended sentence, a fine and a five-year ban from public office. Former Defence minister Guy Coeme and former PS chairman Guy Spitaels received two-year suspended sentences and five-year office bans. Serge Dassault, head of the Dassault group, was convicted of active corruption. It remains the largest political-corruption conviction in modern Belgian history. The judgment was final and not subject to ordinary appeal.

figures.represents: More than 160 million Belgian francs the court found were paid by Agusta and Dassault to the two socialist parties, about €4 million at the fixed conversion rate of 40.3399 BEF to the euro. A court-established figure, not an allegation.

publicMoney.currentStatus: Established by final judgment of the Court of Cassation on 23 December 1998. Punitive fines imposed on individuals were modest and are separate from the bribe amounts above.

documentedOutcome: All twelve defendants convicted (mostly suspended prison terms plus fines; several with five-year bans from public office). Final judgment, no ordinary appeal. Serge Dassault died in 2018.

title: Kazakhgate
subtitle: A settlement law, a Kazakh billionaire, and a parliamentary inquiry
status: INQUIRY FINDINGS; NO CRIMINAL CONVICTION; settlement law annulled
institution: Belgian Chamber of Representatives (inquiry) · Constitutional Court
intended: Belgium adopted a law of 14 April 2011 greatly expanding the out-of-court criminal settlement (transaction penale), allowing settlements even after prosecution had begun.
actual: In June 2011, three Kazakh businessmen under Belgian criminal investigation settled and avoided trial with no finding of guilt. Suspicions that France had lobbied Belgium to pass the settlement law led to a federal parliamentary inquiry, which found French interference 'unacceptable' but could not establish that it influenced Parliament's vote. The Constitutional Court later annulled the 2011 settlement regime.
summary: Three Kazakh businessmen (the 'Kazakh trio'), facing a Belgian money-laundering and fraud investigation, avoided trial in June 2011 by paying a criminal settlement under a new law that broadened the out-of-court transaction penale. Suspicions arose that France, under President Sarkozy, had pressed Belgium to pass that law so one of them, Patokh Chodiev, could be spared, allegedly in connection with arms and helicopter contracts. A federal parliamentary commission of inquiry examined the affair and adopted its final report on 30 March 2018. The commission concluded that French authorities had engaged in 'unacceptable interference' in Belgian judicial proceedings and singled out the role of a Belgian ex-Senate-president acting as a lawyer, but it could NOT establish that this interference influenced Parliament's 2011 vote on the settlement law. These are political findings of a parliamentary inquiry, not criminal convictions. Separately, on 2 June 2016 the Constitutional Court annulled the 2011 extended-settlement regime for lack of effective judicial control. No named individual has a criminal conviction arising from Kazakhgate: the 2011 transaction extinguished the prosecution with no finding of guilt.

figures.classification: Amount paid under the 2011 criminal transaction (settlement, no finding of guilt)
figures.represents: The sum Patokh Chodiev personally paid in the 2011 transaction penale, plus roughly €251,000 in court fees. A settlement figure, not a fine after conviction and not proof of guilt.

figures.classification: Total paid by all seven accused in the 2011 criminal settlement
figures.represents: Penalties and fees across all accused in the 2011 transaction. Distinct from any tax matter.

figures.classification: SEPARATE mid-2000s tax settlement, not the criminal settlement
figures.represents: A widely-cited but different figure: an earlier tax settlement with the Belgian tax authorities. It is often wrongly reported as the Kazakhgate criminal amount. It is not.

publicMoney.currentStatus: Only €522,500 (Chodiev) / €3.5 million (all accused) flowed through the 2011 criminal proceeding, which ended with no finding of guilt. The €23 million tax figure is a separate matter.

documentedOutcome: Parliamentary inquiry report adopted 30 March 2018: French interference judged 'unacceptable', but no proof it influenced the 2011 vote. Constitutional Court (decision no. 83/2016, 2 June 2016) annulled the extended settlement regime. No criminal conviction of any named individual arising from Kazakhgate.

title: The reception crisis (Fedasil)
subtitle: Thousands of court orders to house asylum seekers, largely unenforced
status: STATE REPEATEDLY CONDEMNED; ECtHR violation found (2023); ongoing
institution: Belgian federal State · Fedasil · labour courts · European Court of Human Rights
intended: Provide asylum seekers with the housing and material reception the law requires (a federal competence, delivered through the agency Fedasil).
actual: From 2021 onward Belgium chronically failed to house asylum seekers. Labour courts ordered the State and Fedasil to provide accommodation, backed by daily penalty payments; the State largely did not comply and, per the reported figures, largely did not pay the penalties. In 2023 the European Court of Human Rights found that Belgium's refusal to enforce these orders violated the Convention.
summary: Since 2021 Belgium's federal reception agency, Fedasil, has repeatedly failed to provide asylum seekers with the accommodation and material support the law requires, leaving many on the street. Asylum seekers obtained urgent orders from the labour courts requiring Fedasil to house them, typically backed by a daily penalty payment (astreinte). The State systematically failed to comply. According to an Amnesty International tally (figures as of January 2025), the labour courts had condemned Fedasil 10,407 times since the start of the crisis, with the Brussels labour tribunal alone condemning it more than 5,000 times. Common orders set a penalty of €125 per person per day; on 31 October 2022 the Brussels Court of Appeal imposed a general penalty of €10,000 per day per person denied reception. Per Amnesty, the government has largely not paid these penalties, with total amounts owed estimated above €100 million. On 18 July 2023, in Camara v. Belgium (application no. 49255/22), the European Court of Human Rights held that Belgium had violated Article 6 of the Convention by refusing to execute an enforceable order to house an applicant, finding a systemic failure to enforce reception judgments. This is State and institutional liability, established by courts; it is not a finding of criminal guilt against any named individual.

publicMoney.currentStatus: Penalties were legally imposed but, per the reported figures, largely not paid. The 10,407 condemnations are a count of court decisions, not a sum of money.

documentedOutcome: State repeatedly condemned by the labour courts (10,407 times as of January 2025, per Amnesty). ECtHR found a Convention violation in Camara v. Belgium (18 July 2023). The reception shortfall remained a live issue.

title: Publifin / Nethys (Liege)
subtitle: Sitting fees, an inquiry, and a set of acquittals
status: INQUIRY FINDINGS; ACQUITTALS IN ONE STRAND; OTHER STRANDS PRE-TRIAL (presumed innocent)
institution: Walloon Parliament (inquiry) · Liege judiciary · Publifin / Nethys / Enodia
intended: Publifin was a Liege inter-municipal utility group, majority-owned by the Province of Liege, operating commercially through its subsidiary Nethys (telecoms, energy, media).
actual: In December 2016 it emerged that local politicians drew attendance fees from Publifin 'sector committees' that had become largely useless. Concerns broadened to executive pay and governance. A Walloon Parliament inquiry reported in 2017 and referred possible offences to the prosecutor. In the main criminal strand, seven former board members were definitively acquitted. Separate strands involving former CEO Stephane Moreau remain at the charge / pre-trial stage; he denies wrongdoing and is presumed innocent. No one has been convicted.
summary: Publifin was a Liege-based inter-municipal utility group, majority-owned by the Province of Liege, operating commercially through its subsidiary Nethys (later the group was renamed Enodia). In December 2016 it was revealed that local politicians sat on 'sector committees' that had become functionally useless after mergers, yet still drew attendance fees. The affair broadened to executive remuneration and governance. The Walloon Parliament created an inquiry commission whose final report (6 July 2017) flagged an 'abnormally high' rise in management remuneration and referred fifteen indices of possible offences to the Liege prosecutor. Those are inquiry findings and referrals, not charges or convictions. In the highest-profile criminal strand, on the sector committees, seven former board members went to trial and were acquitted by the Liege tribunal on 19 December 2019; the Court of Appeal confirmed the acquittals on 9 September 2021, and the Court of Cassation rejected the prosecution's appeal on 27 January 2022, making the acquittals final. Former CEO Stephane Moreau was not a defendant in that strand. He was separately charged in 2021 in another dossier and is a referral target in a further 'retention indemnities' dossier for which the prosecutor filed a referral request in 2025; both remain at the charge / pre-trial stage. Moreau denies all wrongdoing and is presumed innocent. As of the latest authoritative information, no Publifin or Nethys figure has been convicted of any offence; the only judicial finality to date is a set of acquittals.

title: Samusocial de Bruxelles
subtitle: Attendance fees at a charity that ran on public money
status: INQUIRY FINDINGS; REFERRED TO TRIAL (2026); NO CONVICTION (presumed innocent)
institution: Brussels COCOM Parliament (inquiry) · Brussels judiciary · Samusocial (ASBL)
intended: Samusocial was a Brussels non-profit providing emergency shelter and aid to homeless people, funded almost entirely by public money.
actual: In 2017 it emerged that board members, including the then Brussels mayor and the CPAS president, had drawn attendance fees from a body living off public subsidies. Both resigned. A Brussels parliamentary inquiry found improper attendance fees and governance failures and sought reimbursement. A criminal investigation followed; in February 2026 five defendants, including the two politicians, were referred to trial. There has been no conviction and they are presumed innocent.
summary: The Samusocial de Bruxelles was a non-profit (ASBL) providing emergency shelter to homeless people, funded almost entirely by public money (about 98% of its income, roughly 10 million euros a year from the Brussels COCOM). In mid-2017 it emerged that board members, including then Brussels mayor Yvan Mayeur and CPAS president Pascale Peraita, had drawn attendance fees for board meetings over several years, in a body overseen by the same political actors it depended on. Both resigned and left the Socialist Party. A Brussels COCOM parliamentary inquiry adopted its final report on 21 February 2018, describing conflicts of interest and role-confusion (which it framed as more ethical than legal) and deficient governance, and it sought reimbursement of the attendance fees: about 346,300 euros in total from twelve administrators, including roughly 112,980 euros from Mayeur and about 113,400 euros from Peraita. Those are parliamentary-inquiry findings, not criminal verdicts. A separate criminal investigation examined possible forgery, embezzlement, misuse of ASBL assets and accounting offences. On 27 February 2026 the chambre du conseil referred five defendants, including Mayeur and Peraita, to the correctional tribunal on those charges. That is a referral to trial only: there has been no conviction, the defendants may still appeal the referral, and they are presumed innocent.
